definition: Consider or hold as true.
example: I cannot accept the dogma of this church.
etymology: First attested about 1380. From Middle English accepten, borrowed from Old French accepter, or directly from Latin acceptō, acceptāre (“receive”), frequentative of accipiō, formed from ad- + capiō (“to take”).

definition: An unfortunate mishap; especially one causing damage or injury.
etymology: First attested in the late 14th century. From Middle English accident, from Old French accident, from Latin accidēns, present active participle of accidō (“happen”); from ad (“to”) + cadō (“fall”). See cadence, case.

definition: Serving temporarily especially as a substitute.
example: The acting president.
etymology: From act + -ing.

definition: Tending to become more severe or wider in scope.
example: Active tuberculosis.
etymology: From Middle English actyf, from Old French actif, from Latin āctīv(us), from agere (“to do, to act”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂éǵeti. By surface analysis, act + -ive.

definition: Any specific behavior.
example: They avoided all recreational activity.
etymology: From Middle French activité, from Latin activitas. Equivalent to active + -ity.

definition: Presently existing in fact and not merely potential or possible.
example: The predicted temperature and the actual temperature were markedly different.

definition: Speak to.

definition: (of animals) fully developed.
example: An adult animal.
etymology: From French adulte, from Latin adultus (“grown up”), perfect passive participle of adolescō (“to grow up”). Compare adolescent.

definition: Farther along in physical or mental development.
example: The child's skeletal age was classified as ‘advanced’.
etymology: From advance + -ed.

definition: A proposal for an appropriate course of action.
example: She was offered various pieces of advice on what to do.
etymology: Mostly displaced native Old English rǣd (see modern rede).

definition: Filled with fear or apprehension.
example: Afraid even to turn his head.

definition: An administrative unit of government.
example: The Central Intelligence Agency.

definition: An active and efficient cause; capable of producing a certain effect.
example: Their research uncovered new disease agents.
etymology: From Latin agēns, present active participle of agere (“to drive, lead, conduct, manage, perform, do”).

definition: Be in accord; be in agreement.
example: We agreed on the terms of the settlement.

definition: United by being of the same opinion.
example: Agreed in their distrust of authority.

definition: A person or thing that is a resource that helps make something easier or possible to do.
example: Visual aids in teaching.
etymology: From Middle English aide, eide, ayde, from Old French eide, aide, from aidier, from Latin adiūtō, adiūtāre (“to assist, help”). Cognates include Spanish ayuda, Portuguese ajuda and Italian aiuto.

definition: Equip with an apparatus for controlling the humidity and temperature.
example: Our house is not air-conditioned.

definition: Drop (an object) from the air; unload from a plane or helicopter.
Transport (cargo) by air.
Possessing life.
example: The happiest person alive.
etymology: From Middle English alyve, alive, alife, olive, olife, on live, on life, from Old English on līfe (“alive”, literally “in life" or "in (the) body”), from on (“on, in”) + līfe, dative singular of līf (“life”).

definition: A contestant who loses the contest.
etymology: From the world of horse race betting, where lists of winners would be published with non-paying positions printed in a block under the heading “Also Ran”.

definition: Marked by the appetites and passions of the body.
example: Animal instincts.
etymology: From Middle English animal, from Latin animālis, from either anima (“breath, spirit”) or animus.

definition: Completing its life cycle within a year.
example: A border of annual flowering plants.
etymology: First attested around 1382 as Middle English annuel, from Late Latin annuālem, annuālis, related to Latin annālis, adjective form of annus (“year”). Used to categorize plants since 1710.

definition: At the present or from now on; usually used with a negative.
example: Alice doesn't live here anymore.
etymology: From any + more.

definition: Used to indicate that a statement explains or supports a previous statement.
example: I don't know what happened to it; anyway, it's gone.
etymology: From any + way.

definition: At or in or to any place.
example: You can find this food anywhere.
etymology: From any + where.

definition: Separated or at a distance in place or position or time.
example: These towns are many miles apart.
etymology: From Middle English apart, aparte, a-part, a part, from Anglo-Norman a part, from Latin ad partem (“to the side”).

definition: Give a certain impression of being something or having a certain aspect.
example: This appears to be a very difficult problem.

definition: Ideas or actions intended to deal with a problem or situation.
example: His approach to every problem is to draw up a list of pros and cons.
etymology: From Middle English approche (“approach, arrival”), from approchen, aprochen (“to come or go near, approach; to adjoin, be close by; to enter (someone’s) presence; to be or become involved; to reach (a certain state);

definition: A person whose creative work shows sensitivity and imagination.
etymology: From French artiste, from Late Latin artista, from ars (“art”). Doublet of artiste. Displaced native Old English cræftiga. By surface analysis, art + -ist.

definition: The verbal act of requesting.
example: His asking was greeted with silence.
etymology: From Middle English askinge, askande, from Old English āsciende, from Proto-West Germanic *aiskōndī, present participle of Proto-West Germanic *aiskōn (“to ask”), equivalent to ask + -ing.

definition: Earnest and conscientious activity intended to do or accomplish something.
example: We made an attempt to cross the stream, but didn’t manage.
etymology: The noun is from the 1530s, the sense "an assault on somebody's life, assassination attempt" (French attentat) is from 1580. By surface analysis, at- + tempt.

definition: A gathering of spectators or listeners at a (usually public) performance.
example: The audience applauded.
etymology: From Middle English audience, from Middle French audience, from Old French audience, from Latin audientia, from present participle audiēns (“hearing”), from verb audiō (“to hear”). Doublet of audiencia.

definition: Writes (books or stories or articles or the like) professionally (for pay).
example: The copyright of any original writing belongs initially and properly to its author.
etymology: From Middle English auctour, from Anglo-Norman autour, from Old French autor, from Latin auctor, from augeō (“to increase, originate”).

definition: Stay clear from; keep away from; keep out of the way of someone or something.
example: Her former friends now avoid her.
etymology: From Middle English avoiden, from Anglo-Norman avoider, Old French esvuidier (“to empty out”), from es- + vuidier, from Vulgar Latin *vocitāre < Vulgar Latin *vocitum, ultimately related to Latin vacuus.

definition: A grant made by a law court.
example: He criticized the awarding of compensation by the court.
etymology: From Middle English awarden, from Anglo-Norman awarder, from Medieval Latin *exwardare, from Latin ex (“out”) + Medieval Latin wardare, guardare (“to observe, regard, guard”); see ward, guard, regard.

definition: Inspiring awe or admiration or wonder.
example: The awesome complexity of the universe.
etymology: From awe + -some; compare earlier awful and Middle English eiful (“inducing fright or terror, terrible”), from Old English eġeful (“fearful; inspiring awe”).

definition: Take watchful responsibility for.
example: I baby-sit the neighbor's plants when she is out of town.

definition: A flexible container with a single opening.
example: He stuffed his laundry into a large bag.

definition: A room or establishment where alcoholic drinks are served over a counter.
example: He drowned his sorrows in whiskey at the bar.
etymology: From Middle English barre, from Old French barre (“beam, bar, gate, barrier”), from Vulgar Latin *barra, of uncertain origin. Doublet of barre.

definition: Pertaining to or constituting a base or basis.
example: A basic fact.
etymology: From base + -ic.

definition: A relation that provides the foundation for something.
example: He worked on an interim basis.
etymology: From Latin basis, from Ancient Greek βάσις (básis), from Proto-Indo-European *gʷémtis, derived from Proto-Indo-European *gʷem- (whence also come). Doublet of base. Displaced native Old English stapol.

definition: An indentation of a shoreline larger than a cove but smaller than a gulf.
example: This hotel has a great view across the bay.
etymology: From French baie, from Late Latin baia, probably ultimately from Iberian or Basque badia. Partly displaced native Old English byht, whence bight.

definition: An area of sand sloping down to the water of a sea or lake.
Damaged by blows or hard usage.
etymology: Deverbal from beat up.

definition: The qualities that give pleasure to the senses.
example: Brigitte Bardot was a renowned beauty.
etymology: From Middle English bewty, bewte, beaute, bealte, from Anglo-Norman and Old French beauté (early Old French spelling biauté), from Vulgar Latin *bellitātem (“beauty”), from Latin bellus (“beautiful, fair”); see beau.

definition: According with custom or propriety.
example: Her becoming modesty.

definition: Take the first step or steps in carrying out an action.
etymology: From Middle English beginnen, from Old English beginnan (“to begin”), from Proto-West Germanic *biginnan, from Proto-Germanic *biginnaną (“to begin”), from be- + base verb *ginnaną also found in Old English onginnan.

definition: Financial assistance in time of need.
example: She can't read, so the voice recording was made for her benefit.

definition: Maintain with or as if with a bet.
example: I bet she will be there!
etymology: From 16th-century criminal slang, perhaps from Middle English bet (“something better, advantage, luck”), from Old English bet, bett (“better”, adverb);

definition: Farther along in space or time or degree.
example: Through the valley and beyond.
etymology: From Middle English biyonde, from Old English beġeondan, from be- + ġeond; related to yonder.

definition: Large or big relative to something else.
example: That whereas, and whereby, and by which, the major, and most greater, and most bigger, and most stronger party, […].

definition: The time when something begins (especially life).
example: They divorced after the birth of the child.
etymology: From Middle English birthen, birðen, from the noun (see above).

definition: An anniversary of the day on which a person was born (or the celebration of it).
etymology: From Middle English birthdai, birtheday, from Old English ġebyrddæġ (“birthday”), influenced by Old Norse burðr, equivalent to birth + day.

definition: A small vessel for travel on water.
example: We can't get everything in the boat. We'll leave this stuff behind.
etymology: Compare typologically ship << Proto-Indo-European *skey-; Russian долблёнка (dolbljónka) (< долби́ть (dolbítʹ)), Russian чёлн (čoln) (akin to коло́ть (kolótʹ)).

definition: A line that indicates a boundary.
etymology: Not cognate to beard, although inside Germanic there may have been influence between the senses of these two roots: see e.g. Old Norse barð (“edge”).

definition: A person who exercises control over workers.
etymology: The video game sense is borrowed from Japanese ボス (bosu), borrowed from English boss.

definition: The lower side of anything.
A name given to a product or service.

definition: The act of breaking something.
example: The breakage was unavoidable.

definition: The act of delivering or distributing something (as goods or mail).
Lacking funds.

definition: Physically and forcibly separated into pieces or cracked or split.
example: A broken mirror.
etymology: From Middle English broken, from Old English brocen, ġebrocen, from Proto-Germanic *brukanaz, past participle of Proto-Germanic *brekaną (“to break”).

definition: A sum of money allocated for a particular purpose.
example: The laboratory runs on a budget of a million a year.

definition: The act of buying.
example: Buying and selling fill their days.
etymology: From buy + -ing.

definition: Unwanted marine creatures that are caught in the nets while fishing for another species.
example: Thousands of dolphins and porpoises and whales are killed as part of the by-catch each year.

definition: A United States bill worth 100 dollars.
etymology: From the Roman numeral C (“100”) (which was printed on it) + note. Attested from the 1920s.

definition: The particular occupation for which you are trained.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English callyng, kallyng, kalland, from Old English *cealliende and Old Norse kallandi, equivalent to call + -ing.

definition: Temporary living quarters specially built by the army for soldiers.
example: Wherever he went in the camp the men were grumbling.
etymology: From Spanish campo (“countryside”).

definition: Capability to perform or produce.
example: Among his gifts is his capacity for true altruism.
etymology: From Middle English capacite, from Old French capacite, from Latin capācitās (whence -acity), from capāx (“able to hold much”), from capiō (“to hold, to contain, to take, to understand”).

definition: An officer holding a rank below a major but above a lieutenant.
etymology: Doublet of chieftain, also from Old French.

definition: A game played with playing cards.
example: He's a fan of cards.

definition: Move while supporting, either in a vehicle or in one's hands or on one's body.
example: You must carry your camping gear.
etymology: From Middle English carien, from Anglo-Norman carier (modern French charrier); from a derivative of Latin carrus (“four-wheeled baggage wagon”), ultimately of Gaulish origin.

definition: Money in the form of bills or coins.
example: There is a desperate shortage of hard cash.
etymology: From late Middle French caisse (“money-box”), itself borrowed from Occitan caissa, from Latin capsa (“box”), ultimately from capiō (“take, seize”), from Proto-Indo-European *kap- (“grasp”).

definition: Put or send forth.
example: Cast a spell.
etymology: The senses relating to broadcasting are based on that same term; compare -cast.

definition: Thrown away.
example: Wearing someone's cast-off clothes.
etymology: Deverbal from cast off.

definition: A fractional monetary unit of several countries.
example: He blew every last cent.
etymology: From Middle English cent, from Old French cent, from Latin centum, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱm̥tóm.

definition: An area that is approximately central within some larger region.
etymology: From Middle English center, centre, from Middle French centre, from Latin centrum, from Ancient Greek κέντρον (kéntron), from κεντεῖν (kenteîn, “to prick, goad”). Doublet of centrum.

definition: The male officer who presides at the meetings of an organization.
etymology: From chair + -man.

definition: Marked by continuous change or effective action.
A path over which electrical signals can pass.
example: A channel is typically what you rent from a telephone company.
etymology: From Middle English chanelen, from the noun (see above).

definition: Pick out, select, or choose from a number of alternatives.
example: Choose a good husband for your daughter.
etymology: From Middle English chesen, from Old English ċēosan (“to choose, seek out, select, elect, decide, test, accept, settle for, approve”), from Proto-West Germanic *keusan, from Proto-Germanic *keusaną (“to test;

definition: Any expected deliverer.
example: False christs will offer false hope and provide no salvation.

definition: Applying to ordinary citizens as contrasted with the military.
example: Civil authorities.

definition: An assertion of a right (as to money or property).
example: His claim asked for damages.

definition: Free from dirt or impurities; or having clean habits.
example: Children with clean shining faces.

definition: Without doubt or question.
example: They were clearly lost.
etymology: From Middle English clerli, clerely, clerelych, cleerliche, clerliche. By surface analysis, clear + (adverbial) -ly.

definition: Not open or affording passage or access.
example: The many closed streets made travel difficult.

definition: A person who closes something.
example: Whoever is the closer has to turn out the lights and lock up.
etymology: From Middle English closere, equivalent to close (verb) + -er.

definition: Clothing in general.
example: He always bought his clothes at the same store.
etymology: See the etymology of the corresponding lemma form.

definition: Sign jointly.
example: Husband and wife co-signed the lease.
etymology: From co- + sign.

definition: Feature as the co-star in a performance.
The shore of a sea or ocean.
example: The rocky coast of Maine has few beaches.
etymology: Compare typologically cape < Latin caput, ness (akin to nose), Bulgarian нос (nos, “nose; …;

definition: A beverage consisting of an infusion of ground coffee beans.
example: He ordered a cup of coffee.
etymology: Borrowed from Dutch koffie, from Italian caffè, from Ottoman Turkish قهوه (kahve), from Arabic قَهْوَة (qahwa).

definition: A visual attribute of things that results from the light they emit or transmit or reflect.
example: A white color is made up of many different wavelengths of light.

definition: An authoritative direction or instruction to do something.
example: I was given a command to cease shooting.
etymology: Compare typologically Russian поручи́ть (poručítʹ), поруче́ние (poručénije), руководи́ть (rukovodítʹ), руководи́тель (rukovodítelʹ) related to рука́ (ruká).

definition: A statement that expresses a personal opinion or belief or adds information.
example: From time to time she contributed a personal comment on his account.
etymology: From Middle English commenten, comenten, from Latin commentārī (“to consider thoroughly, think over, discuss, write upon”).

definition: A conceptual whole made up of complicated and related parts.
example: The complex of shopping malls, houses, and roads created a new town.
etymology: From French complexe, from Latin complexus, past participle of complector (“to entwine, encircle, compass, infold”), from com- (“together”) and plectō (“to weave, braid”). May be analyzed as com- + -plex. See complect.

definition: A machine for performing calculations automatically.
etymology: From compute + -er. Doublet of cantore, counter, and kontor. The sense referring to people first appears c. 1613 in the works of the poet Richard Brathwait. The sense referring to a machine first appears c.

definition: An abstract or general idea inferred or derived from specific instances.
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French concept, from Latin conceptus (“a thought, purpose, also a conceiving, etc.”), from concipiō (“to take in, conceive”). Doublet of conceit and concetto. See conceive.

definition: A meeting of elected or appointed representatives.
etymology: From Latin congress(um), the past participle of congredior (“to go, come together”), itself from con- + gradior (“to go, step”). The verb is from the noun.

definition: Deem to be.
example: I consider her to be shallow.
etymology: From Middle English consideren, from Middle French considerer, from Latin considerare.

definition: Close interaction.
example: They kept in daily contact.
etymology: From Latin contactus, from contingō (“to touch on all sides”), from tangō (“to touch”). Used in English since the 17th century.

definition: Enter into a contractual arrangement.
example: The snail’s body contracted into its shell.

definition: A reproduction of a written record (e.g. of a legal or school record).

definition: A small group of indispensable persons or things.
example: Five periodicals make up the core of their publishing program.
etymology: From Middle English core, kore, coor (“apple-core, pith”), of obscure and uncertain origin.

definition: A place off to the side of an area.
example: He tripled to the rightfield corner.
etymology: From corn + -er. Piecewise doublet of grainer.

definition: Make right or correct.
example: Correct the mistakes.
etymology: From Middle English correcten, borrowed from Anglo-Norman correcter, from Latin correctus.

definition: Pecuniary reimbursement to the winning party for the expenses of litigation.
(criminal law) an act punishable by law; usually considered an evil act.
example: A long record of crimes.
etymology: From Middle English cryme, crime, from Old French crime, crimne, from Latin crīmen. Displaced native Old English firen.

definition: Bringing or deserving severe rebuke or censure.
example: A criminal waste of talent.
etymology: From Middle English cryminal, borrowed from Anglo-Norman criminal, from Late Latin criminalis, from Latin crimen (“crime”).

definition: Marked by a tendency to find and call attention to errors and flaws.
example: A critical attitude.
etymology: From Latin criticus + English -al.

definition: Cause to herd, drive, or crowd together.
example: The man crowded into the packed room.
etymology: (group of people, mob): Compare typologically throng (<<~ Proto-Germanic *þrinhwaną); Czech dav (akin to Russian дави́ть (davítʹ), да́вка (dávka)); Polish ciżba, ścisk (<~ ciskać, akin to ти́скать (tískatʹ));

definition: Of or relating to the arts and manners that a group favors.
example: Cultural events.
etymology: From culture + -al.

definition: Costing less than standard price.
example: Cut-rate goods.

definition: An informal term for a father; probably derived from baby talk.
example: His dad was always there for him.
etymology: From Early Modern English dadd, dadde (circa 1500), undoubtedly older, from unrecorded Middle English *dadde, of uncertain ultimate origin. Compare West Frisian deite (“dad, daddy”), Swabian Dede (“Godfather”).

definition: The occurrence of a change for the worse.
example: The damage is already done.
etymology: From Middle English damage, from Old French damage, from Vulgar Latin *damnāticum from Classical Latin damnum. Compare modern French dommage. Largely displaced native Middle English scath (whence unscathed).

definition: Use of chemical analysis to estimate the age of geological specimens.
example: Janet was surprised at how much casual dating had changed since she was last single.

definition: Make or become free of frost or ice.
etymology: From de- + ice.

definition: Dearly loved.
example: The dearer the jewel, the greater the love expressed.

definition: Reach, make, or come to a decision about something.
example: We finally decided after lengthy deliberations.
etymology: From Middle English deciden, from Old French decider, from Latin dēcīdere, infinitive of dēcīdō (“cut off, decide”), from dē (“down from”) + caedō (“cut”).

definition: Of or taking place in the deeper parts of the sea.
example: Deep-sea fishing.

definition: Having a sunken area.
example: His haggard eyes were deep-set, sunken into their sockets from exhaustion.
etymology: From deep + set.

definition: Toss out; get rid of.
example: Deep-six these old souvenirs!

definition: Request urgently and forcefully.
example: The victim's family is demanding compensation.
etymology: From late Middle English demaunden, from Old French demander, from Latin dēmandō, dēmandāre. Displaced native Old English ġiwian (“to demand”).

definition: Done or made or performed with purpose and intent.
example: Style … is more than the deliberate and designed creation.

definition: True confidential information.
example: After the trial he gave us the real details.

definition: Make something new, such as a product or a mental or artistic creation.
example: Her company developed a new kind of building material that withstands all kinds of weather.

definition: Tradition-bound and obstinately opinionated.
example: An inflexible (or die-hard) conservative.
etymology: Deverbal from die hard.

definition: Displaying numbers rather than scale positions.
example: Digital clock.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin digitālis, from digitus (“finger, toe”) + -alis (“-al”), equivalent to digit + -al. Doublet of digitalis.

definition: Command with authority.
example: He directed the children to do their homework.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin dīrēctus, perfect passive participle of dīrigō (“straighten, direct”), from dis- (“asunder, in pieces, apart, in two”) + regō (“make straight, rule”). Compare dress. Doublet of derecho.

definition: Without deviation.
example: The path leads directly to the lake.
etymology: From direct + -ly.

definition: An impairment of health or a condition of abnormal functioning.
etymology: From Middle English disese, from Anglo-Norman desese, disaise, from Old French desaise, from des- + aise.

definition: The property created by the space between two objects or points.

definition: The 23rd letter of the Roman alphabet.
Cause to move by pulling.
example: Draw a wagon.

definition: A series of mental images and emotions occurring during sleep.
example: I had a dream about you last night.

definition: Put on clothes.
example: We had to dress quickly.

definition: A single serving of a beverage.
example: I asked for a hot drink.

definition: The act of consuming liquids.
example: Some say drinking is a vice.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English [Term?]. By surface analysis, drink + -ing.

definition: Having the power of driving or impelling.
example: A driving personal ambition.
etymology: From Middle English dryvyng, drivende, from Old English drīfende, from Proto-Germanic *drībandz, present participle of Proto-Germanic *drībaną (“to drive”), equivalent to drive + -ing.

definition: Let fall to the ground.
example: Don't drop the dishes.

definition: A noticeable deterioration in performance or quality.
