definition: The social force that binds you to the courses of action demanded by that force.
example: We must instill a sense of duty in our children.
etymology: From Middle English duete, from Middle English dewe + Middle English -te. Equivalent to due + -ty.

definition: Earlier in time; previously.
example: He called me the day before but your call had come even earlier.

definition: With ease (‘easy’ is sometimes used informally for ‘easily’).
example: She was easily excited.
etymology: From Middle English esiliche, equivalent to easy + -ly.

definition: Lying toward or situated in the east.
example: The eastern end of the island.
etymology: From Middle English esturne, esterne, from Old English ēasterne (“eastern”), from Proto-Germanic *austrōnijaz (“eastern”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ews-ro- (“eastern”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ews- (“dawn, east”).

definition: The act of consuming food.
example: I remember when we visited Aunt Martha's house, we had some really good eating!
etymology: From Middle English etynge, from Old English eting.

definition: The system of production and distribution and consumption.
example: Animal economy, vegetable economy.

definition: The boundary of a surface.
example: I have the edge on him.
etymology: From Middle English egge, from Old English eċġ, from Proto-West Germanic *aggju, from Proto-Germanic *agjō, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eḱ- (“sharp”).

definition: The form in which a text (especially a printed book) is published.
example: She wanted a copy of the Clericotes edition, but had to settle for the 1921 edition. She had never liked abridged editions.
etymology: From French édition, from Latin ēditiō, from ēdere (“to publish”).

definition: Property of a personal character that is portable but not used in business.
example: She left some of her personal effects in the house.

definition: Earnest and conscientious activity intended to do or accomplish something.
example: Made an effort to cover all the reading material.
etymology: From Middle French effort, from Old French esfort, deverbal of esforcier (“to force, exert”), from Vulgar Latin *exfortiō, from Latin ex + fortis (“strong”).

definition: Violent or severe weather (viewed as caused by the action of the four elements).
example: They felt the full fury of the elements.

definition: Having come or been brought to a conclusion.
example: The affair is over, ended, finished.

definition: An opposing military force.
example: The enemy attacked at dawn.
etymology: From Middle English enemy, enemye, enmy, borrowed from Old French enemi, anemi (Modern French ennemi), from Latin inimīcus, from in- (“not”) + amīcus (“friend”).

definition: Make certain of.
example: This nest egg will ensure a nice retirement for us.
etymology: From Middle English ensuren, from Anglo-Norman enseurer, from Old French seur (“sure”). Doublet of insure.

definition: To come or go into.
example: The boat entered an area of shallow marshes.
etymology: From Middle English entren, from Old French entrer, from Latin intrō (“enter”, verb), from intrā (“inside”).

definition: To a complete degree or to the full or entire extent; Completely or entirely.
example: Entirely satisfied with the meal.
etymology: From Middle English entyerly, entierly, enterely, entyreliche, equivalent to entire + -ly.

definition: A happening that is distinctive in a series of related events.
Morally bad or wrong.
example: Evil purposes.
etymology: Cognate with Dutch euvel (“evil”), German übel (“bad, evil”), German Low German övel (“evil”), Luxembourgish iwwel (“queasy, nauseous; bad”), Gothic 𐌿𐌱𐌹𐌻𐍃 (ubils, “bad, evil”).

definition: Chemical process in which one atom or ion or group changes places with another.
example: All in all, it was an even exchange.
etymology: From Middle English eschaunge, borrowed from Anglo-Norman eschaunge, from Old French eschange (whence modern French échange), from the verb eschanger, from Vulgar Latin *excambiāre (from Latin ex with Late Latin cambiō).

definition: Have an existence, be extant.
Presently existing.
example: The existing system.

definition: Considered likely or probable to happen or arrive.
example: Prepared for the expected attack.

definition: Make plain and comprehensible.
example: He explained the laws of physics to his students.
etymology: From Middle English explanen, from Old French explaner, from Latin explanō (“to flatten, spread out, make plain or clear, explain”), from ex- (“out”) + planō (“to flatten, make level”), from planus (“level, plain”);

definition: More than is needed, desired, or required.
example: Found some extra change lying on the dresser.

definition: A drop from an eye dropper.
An act that fails.
example: His failure to pass the test.
etymology: From Anglo-Norman failer, from Old French faillir (“to fail”). Equivalent to fail + -ure.

definition: A strong belief in a supernatural power or powers that control human destiny.
example: He lost his faith but not his morality.
etymology: From Middle English faith (also fay), borrowed from Old French fei, feid, from Latin fidem. Doublet of foy. Displaced native Old English ġelēafa, which was also a word for belief.

definition: Widely known and esteemed.
example: A famous actor.
etymology: From Middle English famous, from Anglo-Norman famous, from Latin fāmōsus, equivalent to fame + -ous. Displaced native Old English hlīsful.

definition: Strike out (a batter), (of a pitcher).
example: We enjoyed standing at the edge of the cliff, being fanned by the wind.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English fan, inherited from Old English fann (“a winnowing, fan”), derived from Latin vannus (“fan for winnowing grain”), derived from Proto-Indo-European *h₂weh₁- (“to blow”).

definition: How something is done or how it happens.
example: In an abrasive fashion.

definition: Having an (over)abundance of flesh.
example: He hadn't remembered how fat she was.
etymology: From Middle English fat, fatt, fatte, from the adjective above, and possibly from Old English fǣt (“fat”, recorded once), from Proto-West Germanic *fait, from Proto-Germanic *faitą, *faitaz (“fat”).

definition: Without fat or fat solids.
example: Nonfat or fat-free milk.
etymology: From fat + -free.

definition: Something regarded with special favor or liking.
example: That book is one of my favorites.

definition: A prominent attribute or aspect of something.
example: The map showed roads and other features.
etymology: From Middle English feture, from Anglo-Norman feture, from Old French faiture, from Latin factūra, from Latin factus, from Latin faciō (“do, make”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁- (“to do, put, place, set”).

definition: Emotional or moral sensitivity (especially in relation to personal principles or dignity).
example: The remark hurt his feelings.

definition: The dressed skin of an animal (especially a large animal).
etymology: From Middle English fell, fel, vel, from Old English fel, fell (“hide, skin, pelt”), from Proto-West Germanic *fell, from Proto-Germanic *fellą, from Proto-Indo-European *pél-no- (“skin, animal hide”).

definition: A day or period of time set aside for feasting and celebration.
example: The Reading and Leeds festivals take place on the August bank holiday.
etymology: From Middle English festival (adjective), from Old French festival (“festive”), from Late Latin fēstīvālis, from Latin fēstīvus (“festive”). By surface analysis, festive + -al. Displaced native Old English frēols.

definition: A quantity of liquor equal to one fifth of a United States gallon.
etymology: PIE word *pénkʷe From Middle English fifthe, fifte, fift, from Old English fīfta (“fifth”), from Proto-Germanic *fimftô (“fifth”) or *femftô, equivalent to five + -th (ordinal suffix).

definition: Engaged in or ready for military or naval operations.
example: Review the fighting forces.

definition: Record in a public office or in a court of law.
example: File for divorce.
etymology: From Old French fil (“thread”), from Latin fīlum (“thread”). Doublet of filum.

definition: (usually followed by ‘with’ or used as a combining form) generously supplied with.
example: Theirs was a house filled with laughter.

definition: The act of determining the properties of something, usually by research or calculation.
etymology: From Middle English fyndyng, Old English findincge; equivalent to find + -ing.

definition: (of materials or goods) brought to the desired final state.
example: A finished product.

definition: Marked by firm determination or resolution; not shakable.
example: Firm convictions.
etymology: From Italian firma (“signature”), from firmare (“to sign”), from Latin firmāre (“to make firm, to confirm (by signature)”), from firmus (“firm, stable”).

definition: Be agreeable or acceptable to.
example: It fits the purpose.
etymology: Possibly from Middle English fit (“an adversary of equal power”), of uncertain further origin.

definition: Restore by replacing a part or putting together what is torn or broken.
example: He fixed me with a sickly grin, and said, "I told you it wouldn't work!".
etymology: From Middle English fixen, borrowed from Old French *fixer (attested only as ficher, fichier; > English fitch), from fix (“fastened; fixed”), from Latin fīxus (“immovable; steady; stable; fixed”), from fīgō (“to drive in;

definition: (of a number) having a fixed and unchanging value.
example: Fixed assets.

definition: Having a surface without slope, tilt in which no part is higher or lower than another.
example: A flat desk.
etymology: The algebraic sense was coined by Serre in a 1956 paper, originally as French plat.

definition: A formation of aircraft in flight.
example: Most birds are capable of flight.
etymology: Cognate with West Frisian flecht (“flight”), Dutch vlucht (“flight”), German Flucht (“flight”) (etymology 2).

definition: The inside lower horizontal surface (as of a room, hallway, tent, or other structure).
example: They needed rugs to cover the bare floors.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English floor, floour, flor, flore, flour, flur, vlor, from Old English flōr (“floor, pavement; deck; gangplank”), from Proto-West Germanic *flōr, from Proto-Germanic *flōraz (“ground;

definition: Travel through the air; be airborne.
example: Man cannot fly.
etymology: From Middle English flye (“flying, flight”), from Old English flyġe (“flying, flight”), from Proto-Germanic *flugiz.

definition: A flight at a low altitude (usually of military aircraft) over spectators on the ground.
Moving swiftly.
example: Fast-flying planes.
etymology: From Middle English flyinge, fleyng, fleyinge, fleynge, fleghyng, fleiʒeyng, flyeghynge, equivalent to fly + -ing.

definition: Produced by or subjected to forcing.
example: Forced-air heating.

definition: The trees and other plants in a large densely wooded area.
example: A forest of criticism.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English forest, from Old French forest, from Early Medieval Latin forestis.

definition: For a limitless time.
example: No one can live forever.
etymology: Univerbation of for ever, from Middle English for ever, for evere. By surface analysis, for + ever. First attested in the late 14c., and first attested in the late 17c. as one word. Noun first attested in 1858.

definition: Following the third position; number four in a countable series.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English fourthe, an alteration (due to four) of ferthe, from Old English fēorþa, fēowerþa, from Proto-West Germanic *feurþō, from Proto-Germanic *fedurþô, equivalent to four + -th (ordinal suffix).

definition: Recently made, produced, or harvested.
example: Fresh bread.
etymology: From Middle English fressh, from Old English fersċ (“fresh, pure, sweet”), from Proto-West Germanic *frisk (“fresh”), from Proto-Germanic *friskaz (“fresh”), from Proto-Indo-European *preysk- (“fresh”).

definition: Assets in the form of money.
example: I don’t know if I have the funds for this.

definition: Obtain.
example: Looks like you’ve gained a new friend.
etymology: From dialectal English gen, gin, short for again, agen (“against”); also Middle English gain, gayn, gein, ȝæn (“against”), from Old English gēan, geġn (“against”). More at against.

definition: A plot of ground where plants are cultivated.
Something acquired without compensation.
etymology: From Middle English yifte, ȝift, partly from Old English ġift, ġyft (“giving, consideration, dowry, wedding”) and Old Norse gipt (“gift, present, wedding”); both from Proto-Germanic *giftiz (“gift”).

definition: Showing or causing joy and pleasure; especially made happy.
example: Glad you are here.
etymology: From Middle English glad, gled, from Old English glæd (“shining; bright; cheerful; glad”), from Proto-Germanic *gladaz (“shiny; gleaming; radiant; happy; glossy; smooth;

definition: A brittle transparent solid with irregular atomic structure.
Involving the entire earth; not limited or provincial in scope.
example: Global war.
etymology: From globe + -al; compare French global.

definition: A signal to proceed.
example: You can start as soon as you get the go-ahead from the president.
etymology: Deverbal from go ahead. As a name for footwear, from the fact that one can't easily step backwards wearing them.

definition: Search the internet (for information) using the Google search engine.
example: He googled the woman he had met at the party.
etymology: Back-formation from googly + -le (frequentative suffix (indicating continuousness or repetition) forming verbs).

definition: The head of a state government.
example: The seven members of the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System are nominated by the President and confirmed by the Senate.

definition: A body of students who are taught together.
etymology: Borrowed from Middle French grade (“a grade, degree”), from Latin gradus (“a step, pace, degree”), from Proto-Italic *graðus, from Proto-Indo-European *gʰradʰ-, *gʰredʰ- (“to walk, go”). Doublet of gradus.

definition: Of behavior that is impressive and ambitious in scale or scope.
example: In the grand manner.
etymology: From Middle English grand, grond, graund, graunt, from Anglo-Norman graunt, from Old French grant, from Latin grandis. Doublet of grande and grandee.

definition: Greater in size or importance or degree.
example: For the greater good of the community.
etymology: See the etymology of the corresponding lemma form.

definition: Highest in quality.
Pass into a condition gradually, take on a specific property or attribute; become.
example: Children grow quickly.

definition: A person who keeps watch over something or someone.
example: The prison guard unlocked the door of the cell. After completing the repairs, he replaced the sump guard.
etymology: From Middle English garde, from early Middle French or late Old French guarde (“a guardian, warden, keeper”) (whence modern French garde), from the verb guarder. Doublet of garda, which is from Irish.

definition: Someone employed to conduct others.
etymology: From Middle English guiden, from Old French guider, from Old Occitan guidar, from Frankish *wītan (“to show the way, lead”), from Proto-Germanic *wītaną (“to see, know;

definition: An interior passage or corridor onto which rooms open.
example: The elevators were at the end of the hall.

definition: Be in charge of, act on, or dispose of.
example: This blender can't handle nuts.

definition: Annoy continually or chronically.
example: He is known to harry his staff when he is overworked.
etymology: From Middle English herien, harien, from Old English herġian, from Proto-West Germanic *harjōn, from Proto-Germanic *harjōną, from *harjaz (“army”), from Proto-Indo-European *koryos, from *ker- (“army”).

definition: Having or indicating good health in body or mind; free from infirmity or disease.
example: A rosy healthy baby.

definition: Of comparatively great physical weight or density.
example: A heavy load.
etymology: From Middle English hevy, heviȝ, from Old English hefiġ, hefeġ, hæfiġ (“heavy; important, grave, severe, serious; oppressive, grievous;

definition: An expression of greeting.
example: Every morning they exchanged polite hellos.
etymology: First attested in 1826. From holla, hollo (attested 1588).

definition: An individual quantity of food or drink taken as part of a meal.
example: The helpings were all small.
etymology: From Middle English helping, helpinge, helpynge, equivalent to help + -ing.

definition: To a high degree or extent; favorably or with much respect.
example: Highly successful.
etymology: From Middle English hiȝly, heȝly, heyȝliche, from Old English hēalīce (“highly”), equivalent to high + -ly.

definition: A local and well-defined elevation of the land.
example: They loved to roam the hills of West Virginia.

definition: The act of retaining something.
etymology: From hold + -ing. The sense "holding company" is from Russian холдинг (xolding), itself a pseudo-anglicism derived from an ellipsis of holding company.

definition: Belonging to or derived from or associated with a divine power.
etymology: From Middle English ali, aly, hale, halege, hali, halȝe, hayly, holi, holia, holie, holiȝ, holy, hooly, oli, oly, wholy, woly, from Old English hāleġ, hāliġ (“holy, sacred;

definition: Not disposed to cheat or defraud; not deceptive or fraudulent; marked by truth.
example: Honest lawyers.
etymology: From Middle English honest, honeste (“honourable, appropriate, excellent”), from Old French honeste, from Latin honestus, from honor.

definition: Perform intricate maneuvers while skiing.
A building where travelers can pay for lodging and meals and other services.
Structures collectively in which people are housed.
etymology: See the etymology of the corresponding lemma form.

definition: Being ten more than ninety.
etymology: From Middle English hundred, from Old English hundred, from Proto-Germanic *hundaradą, from *hundą (from Proto-Indo-European *ḱm̥tóm) + *radą (“count”), a neuter variant of *radō (“row, line, series”).

definition: As cold as ice.
example: I'm going to put my coat back on — I'm ice-cold again!
etymology: From Middle English *is-cold, from Old English īsċeald; equivalent to ice + cold.

definition: Free of ice and open to travel.
example: An ice-free channel in the river.
etymology: From ice + -free.

definition: Affected by an impairment of normal physical or mental function.
example: Ill from the monotony of his suffering.
etymology: From Middle English ille (“evil;

definition: An iconic mental representation.
example: Her imagination forced images upon her too awful to contemplate.
etymology: From Middle English ymage, borrowed from Old French image, from Latin imāgō (“a copy, likeness, image”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eym-; the same PIE root is the source of imitari (“to copy, imitate”); see imitate.

definition: Form a mental image of something that is not present or that is not the case.
example: Try to imagine a pink elephant.
etymology: From Middle English ymagynen, from Middle French imaginer, from Latin imāginor, from imāginem, the accusative singular of imāgō (“a copy, likeness, image”).

definition: The striking of one body against another.
example: The hatchet cut the wood on impact.
etymology: Attested since the 17th century, from Latin impāctus.

definition: To make better.
example: The editor improved the manuscript with his changes.
etymology: From Anglo-Norman emprouwer, from Old French en- + prou (“profit”), from Vulgar Latin prode (“advantageous, profitable”).

definition: The financial gain (earned or unearned) accruing over a given period of time.
etymology: From Middle English income, perhaps continuing (in altered form) Old English incyme (“an in-coming, entrance”), equivalent to in- + come.

definition: In truth (often tends to intensify).
example: They said the car would break down and indeed it did.
etymology: From Middle English indede, univerbation of the phrase in dede (“in sooth, in fact”).

definition: Occurring at the beginning.
example: Took the initial step toward reconciliation.
etymology: From Middle French initial or directly from its Latin etymon initiālis (“of the beginning, incipient, initial”), from initium (“a going in, entrance”), from inīre (“to go into, enter”), from in (“in”) + ire (“to go”).

definition: Resulting from one's intentions.
example: Your intended trip abroad.

definition: Of or relating to two people who are married to each other.
A daily written record of (usually personal) experiences and observations.
example: The university's biology department subscribes to half a dozen academic journals.
etymology: From Middle English journal, from Anglo-Norman jurnal (“daily”), from Old French jornel (“day”) (whence modern French journal), from Latin diurnālis, from diurnus (“of the day”).

definition: Determine the result of (a competition).
example: A higher power will judge you after you are dead.
etymology: From Middle English jugen, borrowed from Anglo-Norman juger, from Old French jugier, from Latin iūdicāre. Doublet of judicate. Partly displaced native deem.

definition: The quality of being just or fair.
example: The justice of a description.

definition: Conformity or harmony.
example: His behavior was not in keeping with the occasion.

definition: Evidencing the possession of inside information.
example: A knowing rascal.
etymology: From know + -ing.

definition: A social class comprising those who do manual labor or work for wages.
example: There is a shortage of skilled labor in this field.

definition: A social class comprising those who do manual labor or work for wages.
etymology: From Middle English labor, labour, labur, from Old French labor (modern labeur) and its etymon, Latin labor.

definition: Be without.
example: This soup lacks salt.

definition: A polite name for any woman.
example: A nice lady at the library helped me.

definition: Large or big relative to something else.
etymology: From Middle English largere, equivalent to large + -er.

definition: Up to the immediate present; most recent or most up-to-date.
example: The very latest scientific discoveries.
etymology: From Middle English lateste, from Old English latost, latest, lætest, superlative of læt, whence English late. Doublet of last.

definition: A person who rules or guides or inspires others.
example: Follow the leader.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English ledere, from Old English lǣdere, from Proto-West Germanic *laidijārī, from *laidī (“leading, leadership”) + *-ārī, or from *laid (“leading”) + *-ārī. By surface analysis, lead + -er.

definition: The body of people who lead a group.
example: The national leadership adopted his plan.

definition: Having or showing profound knowledge.
example: A learned jurist.
etymology: From Middle English lerned, lernd, lernyd, equivalent to learn + -ed, which replaced the earlier lered (“taught”), from Old English (ġe)lǣred, past participle of lǣran (“to teach”).

definition: The cognitive process of acquiring skill or knowledge.
example: The department head was also a scholar of great learning.
etymology: From Middle English lernyng, lernynge, from Old English leornung (“learning, study”), from Proto-West Germanic *liʀnungu (“learning”), equivalent to learn + -ing. Cognate with Old Saxon lernunga, German Lernung.

definition: The act of departing.
Towards the side away from the wind.
example: Lee side, lee shore, lee helm.

definition: A written message addressed to a person or organization.
example: Mailed an indignant letter to the editor.
etymology: From Middle English letter, lettre, from Old French letre, from Latin littera (“letter of the alphabet"; in plural, "epistle”).

definition: A room where books are kept.
example: They had brandy in the library.

definition: Be located or situated somewhere; occupy a certain position.
example: The book lies on the table; the snow lies on the roof; he lies in his coffin.
etymology: From Middle English lien, liggen, from Old English liċġan, from Proto-West Germanic *liggjan, from Proto-Germanic *ligjaną, from Proto-Indo-European *legʰ-.

definition: A long stay in bed in the morning.
example: Since I didn't have to go to work, I decided to have a lie-in.
etymology: Deverbal from lie in.

definition: Found pleasant or attractive; often used as a combining form.
example: A well-liked teacher.

definition: A golf course that is built on sandy ground near a shore.
etymology: From Scots links (“sandy, rolling ground near seashore”), linkis, from Old English hlincas (“rising grounds, hills”).

definition: Situated in a particular spot or position.
example: Valuable centrally located urban land.

definition: A point or extent in space; a point or extent in space.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin locatio, locationis (“a placing”), from locare (“to place, put, set, let”), from locus (“a place”). Equivalent to locate + -ion.

definition: A large number or amount.
example: Made lots of new friends.

definition: Appealing to the emotions as well as the eye.
example: It's a lovely day and the sun is shining.
etymology: From Middle English lovely, luvelich, lufli, from Old English luflīċ, luflīc (“amiable, loving, lovable”), equivalent to love + -ly.

definition: That you have the financial means for.
example: Low-cost housing.

definition: (of a garment) having a low-cut neckline.
example: A low-cut neckline.

definition: Restrained in style or quality.
example: A little masterpiece of low-keyed eloquence.
etymology: From low + key.

definition: Used of buildings of one or only a few stories and usually no elevator; low.
example: Looking out over the roofs of low-rise apartment buildings.
etymology: (architecture): A retronym created as an antonym to high-rise.

definition: Your overall circumstances or condition in life (including everything that happens to you).
example: The luck of the Irish.
etymology: From Middle English luk, lukke, from Middle Dutch luc, geluc, gelucke (“good luck, fortune”) or Middle Low German lücke, gelücke (“lot, fortune, fate, luck”), of obscure origin;

definition: Occurring by chance.
example: A lucky escape.
etymology: From Middle English lukky, equivalent to luck + -y. Cognate with Scots lucky (“lucky”), West Frisian lokkich (“lucky, fortunate”), Dutch gelukkig (“lucky, fortunate, happy”).

definition: Any art that invokes supernatural powers.
The bags of letters and packages that are transported by the postal service.
etymology: From Middle English mal, male from Old English māl (“speech, contract, agreement”) from Old Norse mál (“agreement, speech, lawsuit”). Akin to Old English mǣl (“speech”).

definition: Someone who controls resources and expenditures.
Imposing in size or bulk or solidity.
example: Massive oak doors.
etymology: From Middle English massif, from Middle French massif, equivalent to mass + -ive. The Irish sense is possibly derived from Irish mas (“fine, handsome”).

definition: An artist of consummate skill.
example: A master of the violin.
etymology: From mast + -er.

definition: Concerned with worldly rather than spiritual interests.
example: Material possessions.
etymology: From Middle English material, from Late Latin māteriālis, from Latin māteria (“wood, material, substance”), from māter (“mother”).

definition: The message that is intended or expressed or signified.
example: What is the meaning of this sentence?
etymology: From Middle English mening, menyng, equivalent to mean + -ing.

definition: Something that is remembered.
example: Search as he would, the memory was lost.

definition: A remark that calls attention to something or someone.
example: She made frequent mention of her promotion.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English mencioun, mention, from Old French mention, from Latin mentiōnem, accusative of mentiō (“a mention, calling to mind”).

definition: Used in combination to denote the middle.
example: Midmorning.
etymology: Cognate with Dutch midden (“in the middle”), German Mitte (“center, middle, mean”), Icelandic miður (“middle”, adjective), Latin medius (“middle”, noun and adjective). See also middle.

definition: The fielding position in cricket closest to the bowler on the off side.
The fielding position in cricket closest to the bowler on the on side.
Device for converting sound waves into electrical energy.
example: We'll be there in one zero mikes [i.e. ten minutes].
etymology: Alteration of mic, clipping of microphone. Attested since 1927.

definition: Not caught with the senses or the mind.
Mix together different elements.
example: Mix the eggs and milk with the flour until the consistency is smooth.

definition: A mistake that results from taking one thing to be another.
etymology: Deverbal from mix up.

definition: Migratory.
example: A restless mobile society.
etymology: From Middle English, from Old French, from Latin mōbilis (“easy to be moved, moveable”), from moveō (“move”).

definition: In large part; mainly or chiefly.
example: They're mostly good people, although they have made a few mistakes.
etymology: The sense “probably” is a calque from Indian languages such as Tamil அனேகமாக (aṉēkamāka).

definition: A land mass that projects well above its surroundings; higher than a hill.
example: Everest is the highest mountain in the world.

definition: A change of position that does not entail a change of location.
example: Movement is a sign of life.
etymology: From Middle English mevement, from Old French movement (modern French mouvement), from movoir + -ment; cf. also Medieval Latin movimentum, from Latin movere (“move”). Doublet of moment and momentum.

definition: Having or involving or consisting of more than one part or entity or individual.
example: Multiple birth.
etymology: From French multiple, itself from Late Latin multiplus.

definition: Verbal abuse; a crude substitute for argument.
example: Sticks and stones may break my bones but names can never hurt me.

definition: A politically organized body of people under a single government.
example: African nations.
etymology: From Middle English nacioun, nacion, from Old French nacion, from Latin nātiōnem, accusative of nātiō (“nation”). Displaced Old English þēod and Old English cynewīse.

definition: The essential qualities or characteristics by which something is recognized.
example: It is the nature of fire to burn.
etymology: Displaced native Middle English erd (“character, nature, disposition”) from Old English eard (compare German Art (“nature, character, kind, type”));

definition: The cardinal number that is the sum of eight and one.
example: They guaranteed that our Web site would have 99.99% uptime, or four nines.

definition: Without merit; of little or no value or use.
example: A lazy no-count, good-for-nothing goldbrick.
etymology: Probably aphetized form of no-account

definition: A person of no influence.
etymology: From Middle English nobody, no-body, no body. By surface analysis, no (“none, not any”, adjective) + body (“one, person, individual”).

definition: A canonical hour that is the ninth hour of the day counting from sunrise.
etymology: From Middle English none, noon, non (“not one”), from Old English nān (“not one, not any, none”), from Proto-West Germanic *nain, from Proto-Germanic *nainaz (“none, nought, nothing”), equivalent to ne (“not”) + one.

definition: An illegal daily lottery.
example: Numbers of people have visited the fair.

definition: A large body of water constituting a principal part of the hydrosphere.
example: The island is surrounded by ocean.

definition: Advanced in years; (‘aged’ is pronounced as two syllables).
example: My older brother and I are Catholic twins. He’s older by eleven months, not quite a year older than me.

definition: Used of mouth or eyes.
example: His mouth slightly opened.

definition: An open or empty space in or between things.
example: There was a small opening between the trees.
etymology: From Middle English openynge, openande, openand, from Old English openiende, from Proto-West Germanic *opanōndī, from Proto-Germanic *upanōndz, present participle of *upanōną (“to open”), equivalent to open + -ing.

definition: A personal belief or judgment that is not founded on proof or certainty.
example: My opinion differs from yours.
etymology: From English opine + -ion, from Middle English opinion, opinioun, from Anglo-Norman and Middle French opinion, from Latin opīniō, from opīnor (“to opine”). Displaced native Old English wēna.

definition: Involving only main features.
example: The overall pattern of his life.
etymology: From Middle English overall, overal, from Old English ofer eall, ofer ealle (“over all”), equivalent to over + all.

definition: Having an owner; often used in combination.
example: State-owned railways.

definition: (law) someone who owns (is legal possessor of) a business.
example: He is the owner of a chain of restaurants.

definition: A person's partner in marriage.
example: Business partner.

definition: A course of conduct.
example: The path of virtue.
etymology: From Middle English path, peth, from Old English pæþ (“path, track”), from Proto-West Germanic *paþ, from Proto-Germanic *paþaz (“path”).

definition: A person who requires medical care.
example: The number of emergency patients has grown rapidly.
etymology: From Middle English pacient, from Middle French patient, from Old French pacient, from Latin patiens, present participle of patior (“to suffer, endure”), from Proto-Indo-European *peh₁- (“to hate, hurt”).

definition: Yielding a fair profit.
etymology: From pay + -ing.

definition: Involving the body as distinguished from the mind or spirit.
example: Physical exercise.
etymology: Borrowed from Late Latin physicālis, from Latin physica (“study of nature”), from Ancient Greek φυσική (phusikḗ), feminine singular of φυσικός (phusikós, “natural; physical”), from φύσις (phúsis, “origin, birth;

definition: Situated in a particular spot or position.
example: Strategically placed artillery.

definition: An aircraft that has a fixed wing and is powered by propellers or jets.
example: The flight was delayed due to trouble with the airplane.
etymology: From Latin plānum (“flat surface”), a noun use of the neuter of plānus (“plain”). The word was introduced in the 17th century to distinguish the geometrical senses from the other senses of plain.

definition: An act of formulating a program for a definite course of action.
example: The planning was more fun than the trip itself.

definition: A box for a child's toys and personal things (especially at a boarding school).
A full supply.
example: There was plenty of food for everyone.

definition: Social relations involving intrigue to gain authority or power.
example: Office politics is often counterproductive.
etymology: From politic + -s. By analogy with Aristotle’s τά πολῑτῐκᾱ́ (tá polītĭkā́, “affairs of state”), a plural noun phrase.

definition: Put or turn on the left side, of a ship.
example: Port the helm.
etymology: From Old English port, borrowed from Latin portus (“port, harbour”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *pértus (“crossing”) (and thus a distant doublet of ford).

definition: Characterized by or displaying affirmation or acceptance or certainty etc.
example: A positive attitude.
etymology: From Old French positif, from Latin positivus, from the past participle stem of ponere (“to place”). Compare posit.

definition: By chance.
example: We may possibly run into them at the concert.
etymology: From possible + -ly.

definition: Publicly displayed.
example: The posted speed limit.

definition: Having great power or force or potency or effect.
example: The most powerful government in western Europe.
etymology: From Middle English pouerful, powarfull. By surface analysis, power + -ful.

definition: A social gathering before a party or a sports game.
Made ready or fit or suitable beforehand.
example: A prepared statement.
etymology: From prepare + -ed.

definition: Keep from happening or arising; make impossible.
example: I brush my teeth regularly to prevent tooth decay.
etymology: From Middle English preventen (“anticipate”), from Latin praeventus, perfect passive participle of praeveniō (“to anticipate”), from prae (“before”) + veniō (“to come”).

definition: Of first rank or importance or value; direct and immediate rather than secondary.
example: Primary goals.
etymology: Borrowed from Latin prīmārius (“of the first (rank); chief, principal; excellent”), from prīmus (first; whence the English adjective prime) + -ārius (whence the English suffix -ary);

definition: Earlier in time.
example: His prior residence was smaller than his current one.
etymology: The adjective is a learned borrowing from Latin prior (“earlier, former, previous, prior; in front;

definition: A correctional institution where persons are confined while on trial or for punishment.
example: The cold stone walls of the prison had stood for over a century.
etymology: From Middle English prisoun, prison, from Old English prisūn, a borrowing from Old French prison, from Latin prehensiōnem, accusative singular of prehensiō, from the verb prehendō. Doublet of prehension.

definition: An athlete who plays for pay.
example: What are the pros and cons of buying a car?
etymology: From Late Middle English pro, from Latin prō (“on behalf of”).

definition: Bring forth or yield.
example: The tree would not produce fruit.
etymology: From the verb.

definition: Gradual improvement or growth or development.
example: Great progress in the arts.
etymology: From the noun. Lapsed into disuse in the 17th century, except in the US. Considered an Americanism on reintroduction to use in the UK.

definition: Make a promise or commitment.
example: If you promise not to tell anyone, I will let you have this cake for free.

definition: Marked by suitability or rightness or appropriateness.
example: Proper medical treatment.
etymology: From Middle English propre, from Anglo-Norman proper, propre, Old French propre (French: propre), from Latin proprius.

definition: Shield from danger, injury, destruction, or damage.
example: Weatherbeater protects your roof from the rain.

definition: Be shown or be found to be.
example: She proved to be right.
etymology: Simple past form of proove, conjugated as a Germanic strong verb, on the pattern of choose → chose.

definition: Cause to move by pulling.
example: Pull a sled.
etymology: Verb from Middle English pullen, from Old English pullian (“to pull, draw, tug, pluck off”), of uncertain ultimate origin.

definition: A roadside cafe especially for lorry drivers.
etymology: Deverbal from pull in.

definition: Designated paved area beside a main road where cars can stop temporarily.
etymology: From the phrasal verb pull off.

definition: A roadside cafe especially for lorry drivers.
etymology: Deverbal from pull up.

definition: The acquisition of something for payment.
example: They closed the purchase with a handshake.
etymology: From Middle English purchasen, from Anglo-Norman purchacer (“seek to obtain”) from pur- (from Latin pro-) + chac(i)er (“to chase, pursue”).

definition: An anticipated outcome that is intended or that guides your planned actions.
example: What is the purpose of your visit?
etymology: From Middle English purpos, from Old French purposer (“to propose”) (with conjugation altered based on poser), from Latin prō- (“forth”) + pōnere (“place, put”), hence Latin prōpōnō, prōpōnere.

definition: Move with force.
example: He pushed the table into a corner.
etymology: From Middle English pushen, poshen, posson, borrowed from Middle French pousser (Modern French pousser) from Old French poulser, from Latin pulsare (“to beat, strike”), frequentative of pellere (past participle pulsus).

definition: Hitting a golf ball that is on the green using a putter.
example: His putting let him down today.
etymology: From put + -ing.

definition: One of four equal parts.
example: A quarter of a pound.
etymology: From Middle English quarter, from Anglo-Norman quarter, from Latin quartarius, from quartus. Compare Spanish cuarto (“room, quarters; quarter”). Doublet of quartier.

definition: Accomplished rapidly and without delay.
example: Was quick to make friends.

definition: Raise the level or amount of something.
example: Raise my salary.
etymology: Borrowed from Old Norse hreysi; the spelling came about under the influence of the folk etymology that derived it from the verb.

definition: Located or moved above the surround or above the normal position.
example: A raised design.

definition: Not widely known; especially valued for its uncommonness.
example: A rare word.
etymology: From Middle English rare, from Old French rare, rere (“rare, uncommon”), from Latin rārus (“loose, spaced apart, thin, infrequent”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁reh₁- (“friable, thin”).

definition: A local tax on property.
example: Nonetheless, it did not stop the Fed from cutting rates last Thursday.

definition: Reach a destination, either real or abstract.
example: The water reached the doorstep.
etymology: From Middle English rechen, from Old English rǣċan (“to reach”), from Proto-West Germanic *raikijan, from Proto-Germanic *raikijaną, from the Proto-Indo-European *Hreyǵ- (“to bind, reach”).

definition: All of your experiences that determine how things appear to you.
example: For them demons were as much a part of reality as trees were.
etymology: From French réalité (“quality of being real”), from Middle French realité (“property, possession”), from Medieval Latin reālitās, from Late Latin reālis (“real”), equivalent to real + -ity.

definition: Be fully aware or cognizant of.
Get something; come into possession of.
example: Receive payment.
etymology: From Middle English receyven, from Old French receivre, from Latin recipere (“take back, accept, etc.”), from re- (“back”) + capiō (“to take”); see capacious. Compare conceive, deceive, perceive.

definition: Travel on an overnight flight.
example: The candidate red-eyed from California to the East Coast the night before the election to give a last stump speech.
etymology: The noun is derived from red + eye; sense 2.3 (“strong but poor-quality whiskey”) and sense 3 (“overnight airplane flight”) are probably so named because they may cause people to develop bloodshot eyes.

definition: Characteristic of a region.
example: Regional flora.
etymology: From Middle French régional, from Latin regiōnālis, equivalent to region + -al.

definition: In accordance with fixed order or procedure or principle.
example: His regular calls on his customers.

definition: A strong belief in a supernatural power or powers that control human destiny.
etymology: From Middle English religioun, from Old French religion, from Latin religiō (“scrupulousness, pious misgivings, superstition, conscientiousness, sanctity, an object of veneration, cult-observance, reverence”).

definition: Stay the same; remain in a certain state.
example: The dress remained wet after repeated attempts to dry it.
etymology: From Middle English remainen, from Old French remain-, stressed stem of remanoir, from Latin remaneō, maneō, from Proto-Indo-European *men- (“to stay”).

definition: Any object that is left unused or still extant.
example: I threw out the remains of my dinner.

definition: Separated in relationship by a given degree of descent.
example: A cousin once removed.

definition: Express the need or desire for.
example: She requested an extra bed in her room.

definition: Require as useful, just, or proper.
example: Success usually requires hard work.
etymology: From Old French requerre (whence Modern French requérir), from Latin requīrō (“to require, seek, ask for”, literally “to seek back”), from re- (“back; again”) + quaerō (“to seek”, whence query).

definition: Possessing material wealth.
example: Her father is extremely rich.

definition: Move upward.
example: We watched the balloon rise.
etymology: From Middle English risen, from Old English rīsan, from Proto-West Germanic *rīsan, from Proto-Germanic *rīsaną (“to rise”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁rey- (“to arise, rise”).

definition: Move by turning over or rotating.
example: The child rolled down the hill.
etymology: From Middle English rollen, partly from Old French roller, roler, röeler, röoler, from Medieval Latin rotulāre (“to roll; to revolve”), from Latin rotula (“a little wheel”), diminutive of rota (“a wheel”);

definition: Any of many shrubs of the genus Rosa that bear roses.
etymology: From Middle English rose, roose, from Old English rōse, but with its vowel influenced by Old French rose, both from Latin rosa.

definition: Of a deep slightly bluish red color.
A principle or condition that customarily governs behavior.
example: It was his rule to take a walk before breakfast.
etymology: From Middle English reulen, rulen, borrowed from Old French riuler, from Latin regulāre (“to regulate, rule”), from regula (“a rule”); see regular and regulate.

definition: A particular instance of selling.
example: He has just made his first sale.
etymology: From Middle English sale, from Old English sala (“act of selling, sale”), from Old Norse sala (“sale”), from Proto-Germanic *salō (“delivery”), from Proto-Indo-European *selh₁- (“to grab”).

definition: The place where some action occurs.
example: The police returned to the scene of the crime.
etymology: From Late Middle English scene, from Middle French scene, borrowed from Latin sc(a)ena, from Ancient Greek σκηνή (skēnḗ, “scene, stage”). Doublet of scena and skene.

definition: The activity of looking thoroughly in order to find something or someone.
example: With only five minutes until we were meant to leave, the search for the keys started in earnest.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English serchen, borrowed from Anglo-Norman sercher, Old French cerchier, from Late Latin circō, ,circāre (“to circle; go around; search for”), from circus.

definition: Not open or public; kept private or not revealed.
example: A secret formula.
etymology: The noun is from Middle English secret, from Latin sēcrētum. Doublet of secretum. Displaced Old English dēagolnes (“a secret”). The verb is from the noun.

definition: Exchange or deliver for money or its equivalent.
example: She sells her body to survive and support her drug habit.
etymology: From Middle English sellen, from Old English sellan (“give; give up for money”), from Proto-West Germanic *salljan, from Proto-Germanic *saljaną, from Proto-Indo-European *selh₁-.

definition: The exchange of goods for an agreed sum of money.
example: Buyings and sellings.

definition: Assembly possessing high legislative powers.
Older; higher in rank; longer in length of tenure or service.
example: Senior officer.
etymology: From Middle English senior, from Latin senior (“older”), comparative form of senex (“old”); see senate. Doublet of seigneur, seignior, senhor, señor, senyor, signore, sir, and sire.

definition: Act as a barrier between; stand between.
example: Separate the articles from the headings.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English separat (“separated”), from Latin sēparātus, see -ate (“adjective-forming suffix”) and Etymology 1 for more.

definition: The context and environment in which something is set.
example: The perfect setting for a ghost story.

definition: The act of firing a projectile.
example: His shooting was slow but accurate.
etymology: From Middle English shoting, schoting, from Old English scotung (“shooting”), from Proto-Germanic *skutungō, equivalent to shoot + -ing.

definition: Do one's shopping.
example: She goes shopping every Friday.
etymology: From Middle English shoppe, schoppe, from Old English sċoppa (“shed; booth; stall; shop”), from Proto-Germanic *skupp-, *skup- (“barn, shed”), from Proto-Indo-European *skub-, *skup- (“to bend, bow, curve, vault”).

definition: The display of a motion picture.
example: We went to the midnight showing of the new horror movie.
etymology: From Middle English schewyng, schewinge, from Old English sċēawung (“a looking at, contemplation, consideration; respect, regard; survey, examination;

definition: Move so that an opening or passage is obstructed; make shut.
example: Shut the window.
etymology: Variation of chute or shute (archaic, related to shoot) from Old English scēotan.

definition: Somewhat introverted.
etymology: Deverbal from shut in.

definition: Having a handwritten signature.
example: A signed letter.

definition: A female person who has the same parents as another person.
example: My sister married a musician.
etymology: The sense for "Adelpha-genus butterfly" is a semantic loan from translingual Adelpha, itself from Ancient Greek ἀδελφή (adelphḗ, “sister”).

definition: A strike in which workers refuse to leave the workplace until a settlement is reached.
example: I need a sit-down and a nice cup of tea.
etymology: Deverbal from sit down.

definition: A form of civil disobedience in which demonstrators occupy seats and refuse to move.
etymology: A deverbal from sit in. By surface analysis, sit + -in (protest).

definition: (photography) the act of assuming a certain position (as for a photograph or portrait).
example: He wanted his portrait painted but couldn't spare time for the sitting.
etymology: From Middle English sittyng, sittynge, equivalent to sit + -ing. Cognate with Dutch zitting (“a sitting, session”), German Sitzung (“a sitting, session”), Swedish sittning (“a sitting, session”).

definition: A pistol with a revolving cylinder (usually having six chambers for bullets).
To a small degree or extent.
example: The children argued because one slice of cake was slightly larger than the other.
etymology: From slight + -ly.

definition: Small or little relative to something else.
example: The worse things get, the smaller your focus should be.

definition: Showing mental alertness and calculation and resourcefulness.
example: A smart outfit.
etymology: From Middle English smerten, from Old English *smeortan (“to smart”), from Proto-West Germanic *smertan, from Proto-Germanic *smertaną (“to hurt, ache”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)merd- (“to bite, sting”).

definition: Someone who works at something specified.
etymology: From Middle English smythen (“to work metal, forge, beat into, torment, refine (of God - to refine his chosen);

definition: Disposed of to a purchaser.
example: This merchandise is sold.
etymology: From Middle English solde, sould, soud, from Middle French solde, Italian soldo. Compare soldier and Danish sold (via Low German). Doublet of sol, soldo, solid, solidus, sou, and xu.

definition: Having taken a bribe or bribes.
example: A sold-out politician.
etymology: From sell out.

definition: Characterized by good substantial quality.
example: Solid comfort.
etymology: From Middle English solide, borrowed from Old French solide, from Latin solidus (“solid”), from Proto-Indo-European *solh₂-i-dʰ-o-s (“entire”), suffixed form of root *solh₂- (“integrate, whole”).

definition: The immaterial part of a person; the actuating cause of an individual life.
example: Fifty souls were lost when the ship sank.
etymology: Borrowed from French souler (“to satiate”).

definition: Capable of or involving speech or speaking.
example: Human beings — the speaking animals.
etymology: From Middle English speking, spekynge, equivalent to speak + -ing.

definition: (biology) taxonomic group whose members can interbreed.
example: The male species.
etymology: From Latin speciēs (“appearance; quality”), from speciō (“see”) + -iēs suffix signifying abstract noun. Doublet of spice.

definition: The act of delivering a formal spoken communication to an audience.
example: He had a bad speech impediment.
etymology: From Middle English speche, from Old English spǣċ, sprǣċ (“speech, discourse, language”), from Proto-West Germanic *sprāku (“speech, language”), from Proto-Indo-European *spereg-, *spreg- (“to make a sound”).

definition: Use up a period of time in a specific way.
example: How are you spending your summer vacation?
etymology: Cognate with Old High German spentōn (“to consume, use, spend”) (whence German spenden (“to donate, provide”)), Middle Dutch spenden (“to spend, dedicate”), Old Icelandic spenna (“to spend”).

definition: The act of spending or disbursing money.
example: Excessive spendings.
etymology: From Middle English spendyng, spendynge, from Old English spendung (“spending”), equivalent to spend + -ing. Cognate with German Spendung (“contribution, donation”).

definition: The vital principle or animating force within living things.
example: A wandering spirit haunts the island.
etymology: From Middle English spirit, from Old French espirit (“spirit”), from Latin spīritus (“breath; spirit”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)peys- (“to blow, breathe”).

definition: An active diversion requiring physical exertion and competition.
A point located with respect to surface features of some region.
example: A bright spot on a planet.

definition: Process or result of distributing or extending over a wide expanse of space.
example: November 29, 1712, Andrew Freeport, a letter to The Spectator I have got a fine spread of improvable lands.
etymology: From Middle English spreden, from Old English sprǣdan (“to spread, expand”), from Proto-Germanic *spraidijaną (“to spread”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)per- (“to strew, sow, sprinkle”).

definition: Having a supporting base.
example: A standing lamp.
etymology: From Middle English standyng, stonding, stondung, from Old English *standung, equivalent to stand + -ing.

definition: Declared as fact; explicitly stated.
example: Stated preaching.

definition: The relative position or standing of things or especially persons in a society.
example: He had the status of a minor.
etymology: A learned borrowing from Latin status. A doublet of state and estate. Displaced native Old English hād (“rank, status”).

definition: A flight of stairs or a flight of steps.
example: She followed the steps of the girl beside her.

definition: Put, fix, force, or implant.
example: Stick your thumb in the crack.
etymology: Cognate with Dutch stek (“home, spot; cutting, a leaf, stem, branch, or root removed from a plant and cultivated to grow a new plant”), German Stecken (“stick”), Vilamovian śtakia (“stick”);

definition: Of something (a paper label or postage stamp) gummed in advance.
example: Stick-on labels.

definition: A lump or mass of hard consolidated mineral matter.
etymology: From Middle English stonen, stanen, from Old English *stānian (“to stone”), from Proto-West Germanic *stainōn, from Proto-Germanic *stainōną (“to stone”).

definition: (of a nose) blocked.
example: A stopped (or stopped-up) nose.
etymology: From stop + -ed. In some senses, the adjective follows from the verb; in others, it may derive directly from the noun stop.

definition: Lacking or marked by lack of intellectual acuity.
example: It got trapped in the fishing net because it's a big stupid jellyfish!

definition: The subject matter of a conversation or discussion.
example: He didn't want to discuss that subject.
etymology: From Latin subiectus (“a subject, an inferior”), subiectum (“the subject of a proposition”), past participle of subiciō (“throw, lay, place”), from sub (“under, at the foot of”) + iaciō (“throw, hurl”).

definition: Make a proposal, declare a plan for something.
example: Are you suggesting that I killed my wife?
etymology: Coined based on Latin suggestus, perfect passive participle of suggerō (“bring up, bring under, lay beneath, furnish, supply, excite, advise, suggest”, verb), from sub (“from below, under”) + gerō (“bear, carry”, verb).

definition: Give something useful or necessary to.
example: To supply money for the war.
etymology: From Middle English supplien, borrowed from Old French soupleer, souploier, from Latin suppleo (“to fill up, make full, complete, supply”). The Middle English spelling was modified to conform to Latin etymology.

definition: Required or under orders.
example: I'm supposed to be there at ten.

definition: Having or denoting the characteristic taste of sugar.
example: A sweet apple.
etymology: Cognate with Yola sweet (“sweet”), Saterland Frisian swäit (“sweet”), West Frisian swiet (“sweet”), Alemannic German süeß (“sweet”), Bavarian siaß (“sweet;

definition: A reference point to shoot at.
A beverage made by steeping tea leaves in water.
example: Iced tea is a cooling drink.
etymology: First appears c. 1655, in the English translation Álvaro Semedo’s writings. From Dutch thee, from Hokkien 茶 (tê) (Amoy dialect), from Old Chinese, ultimately from Proto-Sino-Tibetan *s-la (“leaf, tea”).

definition: A person whose occupation is teaching.
etymology: From Middle English techere, equivalent to teach + -er. More at teach.

definition: The profession of a teacher.
example: He prepared for teaching while still in college.
etymology: From Middle English teching, techinge, from Old English tǣċing, tǣċung (“instruction, direction, teaching”), equivalent to teach + -ing.

definition: Disclosing unintentionally something concealed.
example: A telling smile.
etymology: Gerund from the verb tell, from tell + -ing.

definition: Causing fear or dread or terror.
example: A terrible curse.
etymology: Displaced Old English atol and sliþe, while also largely overtaking grimm.

definition: (rugby) an act or instance of throwing a ball in to put it into play.
example: Salesman: Uh, hey, how about a Skinny Scan 27,000 with a Computer Virus Eradicator as a throw-in?
etymology: Deverbal from throw in.

definition: (used to introduce a logical conclusion) from that fact or reason or as a result.
example: It is late and thus we must go.

definition: To a complete degree or to the full or entire extent; Completely or entirely.
example: A totally new situation.
etymology: From total + -ly.

definition: Make physical contact with, come in contact with.
example: Touch the stone for good luck.
etymology: From Middle English touchen, tochen, from Old French tochier (“to touch”) (whence Modern French toucher;

definition: Not given to gentleness or sentimentality.
example: A tough character.
etymology: From Middle English tough, towgh, tou, toȝ, from Old English tōh (“tough, tenacious, holding fast together; pliant; sticky, glutinous, clammy”), from Proto-West Germanic *tą̄h(ī), from Proto-Germanic *tanhuz (“fitting;

definition: A journey or route all the way around a particular place or area.
example: They took an extended tour of Europe.
etymology: From Old French tour, tourn, from the verb torner, tourner.

definition: Create by training and teaching.
example: The old master is training world-class violinists.
etymology: For the meaning to teach compare typologically Russian ната́скивать (natáskivatʹ) (akin to тащи́ть (taščítʹ)).

definition: Transfer somebody to a different position or location of work.
example: To transfer the laws of one country to another; to transfer suspicion.
etymology: From Latin trānsferō (“to bear across”). Distant doublet of translate. See also collate and confer, delate and defer, as well as prelate and prefer among others.

definition: Interact in a certain way.
example: Treat him with caution, please.
etymology: From Middle English treten, from Anglo-Norman treter, Old French tretier, traiter, from Latin tractāre (“to pull", "to manage”), from the past participle stem of trahere (“to draw", "to pull”).

definition: Subjected to a physical (or chemical) treatment or action or agent.
example: The sludge of treated sewage can be used as fertilizer.

definition: Force a person or an animal into a position from which they cannot escape.
example: The dog treed the cat.
etymology: Replaced alternative Middle English beem, from Old English bēam (see beam) and eclipsed non-native Middle English arbre, borrowed from Old French arbre.

definition: The act of testing something.
example: In the experimental trials the amount of carbon was measured separately.
etymology: From Middle English trial, triall, from Anglo-Norman trial, triel, from trier (“to pick out, cull”) + -al. More at English try.

definition: A journey for some purpose (usually including the return).
example: He took a trip to the shopping center.
etymology: From Middle English trippen (“tread or step lightly and nimbly, skip, dance”), perhaps from Old French triper (“to hop or dance around, strike with the feet”), from a Frankish source;

definition: An unintentional but embarrassing blunder.
example: He arranged his robes to avoid a trip-up later.

definition: A source of difficulty.
example: One trouble after another delayed the job.

definition: In accordance with truth or fact or reality.
example: She was now truly American.
etymology: From Middle English truely, treuly, treuli, trewely, treoweliche, treowliche, from Old English trēowlīċe (“faithfully; truly”), equivalent to true + -ly.

definition: Produce a sound as if from a trumpet.
example: He knew the hand was lost when his ace was trumped.
etymology: Possibly from French triomphe (“triumph”) or Old French triumphe. If so, it is a doublet of triumph and thriambus. Compare German Trumpf.

definition: The act of changing or reversing the direction of the course.
example: Take the second turning on the left.
etymology: From Middle English turnyng, turnynge, from Old English tyrning, turnung, equivalent to turn + -ing.

definition: Two times.
example: I called her twice.
etymology: From earlier twise, from Middle English twies, twiȝes, from Old English twīġes (“twice”), from twīwa, twīġa ("twice"; whence Middle English twie (“twice”)) + -es (adverbial genitive ending).

definition: A series of chirps.
example: I often listen to the twitter of the birds in the park.
etymology: From Middle English twitren, twiteren, from Old English *twiterian, from Proto-West Germanic *twitwiʀōn, from Proto-Germanic *twitwizōną (“to chirp; twitter”).

definition: A rented car.
Complete reversal of direction of travel.
Radically distinctive and without equal.
example: Bach was unique in his handling of counterpoint.
etymology: Borrowed from French unique, from Latin unicus.

definition: The topmost one of two; upper.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English upper. By surface analysis, up + -er.

definition: Being of use or service.
example: The girl felt motherly and useful.
etymology: From use + -ful.

definition: A long depression in the surface of the land that usually contains a river.
etymology: From Middle English valeye, valey, from Anglo-Norman valey, Old French valee (compare French vallée), from Latin vallēs/vallis. Doublet of vlei and vly.

definition: A collection containing a variety of sorts of things.
example: He had a variety of disorders.
etymology: * Italian varietà (“difference; variety”)

definition: A conveyance that transports people or objects.
example: Kinetic kill vehicle.
etymology: Borrowed from French véhicule, from Latin vehiculum (“a carriage, conveyance”), from vehō, vehere (“to carry”).

definition: Moral weakness.
example: Pride is a vice, not a virtue.

definition: A successful ending of a struggle or contest.
example: A narrow victory.
etymology: The noun is derived from Middle English victory, victori, victorie (“supremacy, victory; a defeat or vanquishing, conquest; superior military force; might, power, strength; triumphal celebration or procession;

definition: An act of aggression (as one against a person who resists).
example: He may accomplish by craft in the long run what he cannot do by force and violence in the short one.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English violence, borrowed from Old French violence, a learned borrowing from Latin violentia, from violēns /violentus (“violent”) + -ia. See violent. Displaced native Old English stræc.

definition: Be awake, be alert, be there.
example: Command unto the guards that they diligently wake.
etymology: A merger of two verbs of related/similar form and meaning: * Middle English waken, Old English wacan, from Proto-West Germanic *wakan, from Proto-Germanic *wakaną.

definition: Close enough to be walked to.
example: Walking distance.

definition: Be dressed in.
example: She was wearing yellow that day.
etymology: Originally a weak verb (i.e. with a past tense in -ed), it became irregular during the Middle English period by analogy with verbs like beren (whence bear) and teren (whence tear).

definition: Face and withstand with courage.
example: To weather a cape to weather another ship.
etymology: From Middle English weder, wedir, from Old English weder, from Proto-West Germanic *wedr, from Proto-Germanic *wedrą, from Proto-Indo-European *wedʰrom (=*we-dʰrom), from *h₂weh₁- (“to blow”).

definition: An intricate network suggesting something that was formed by weaving or interweaving.
example: The trees cast a delicate web of shadows over the lawn.

definition: The social event at which the ceremony of marriage is performed.
example: The wedding of our three companies took place last week.
etymology: From Middle English wedding, weddynge, from Old English weddung (“betrothal, espousal”), equivalent to wed + -ing. Cognate with Middle Dutch weddinghe.

definition: Suggesting the operation of supernatural influences.
example: The three weird sisters.
etymology: From Middle English werde, wierde, wirde, wyrede, wurde, from Old English wyrd (“fate”), from Proto-West Germanic *wurdi, from Proto-Germanic *wurdiz, from Proto-Indo-European *wert- (“to turn, wind”).

definition: Accept gladly.
example: I welcome your proposals.
etymology: and also in Romance languages, such as Italian benvenuto, Spanish bienvenido, French bienvenu, Catalan benvingut, Portuguese bem-vindo and Romanian bun venit, meaning “[may you have fared] well [in] coming [here]”.

definition: Having ample fabric.
Marked by extreme lack of restraint or control.
example: Wild parties.

definition: Disposed or inclined toward.
example: A willing participant.
etymology: * (adjective): Old English willende, present participle of willan * (noun): Old English willung, from willian By surface analysis, will + -ing.

definition: Fermented juice (of grapes especially).
example: Wine is usually stronger than beer.
etymology: Cognate with Saterland Frisian Wien, West Frisian wyn, Dutch wijn, German Wein, Danish, Norwegian Bokmål, Norwegian Nynorsk, and Swedish vin, Faroese and Icelandic vín.

definition: The contestant who wins the contest.
etymology: Inherited from Middle English wynner, wynnere, equivalent to win + -er.

definition: Having won.
example: The winning team.

definition: The feeling aroused by something strange and surprising.
example: Wonders of the World seem to come in sevens.
etymology: From Middle English wonder, wunder, from Old English wundor (“wonder, miracle, marvel”), from Proto-West Germanic *wundr, from Proto-Germanic *wundrą.

definition: (comparative of ‘bad’) inferior to another in quality or condition or desirability.
example: This road is worse than the first one we took.
etymology: From Middle English worse, werse, from Old English wiersa, from Proto-West Germanic *wirsiʀō, from Proto-Germanic *wirsizô. Cognate with Dutch wers (“worse”).

definition: The least favorable outcome.
example: The worst that could happen.
etymology: From Middle English worste, wurste, warste, werste, wirste, from Old English wierrest, from Proto-Germanic *wirsistaz, superlative form of *ubilaz (“bad, evil”); compare worse.

definition: A joke that seems extremely funny.
etymology: Attested since the 16th century; borrowed from Scots wow; ultimately a natural exclamation.

definition: A young person (especially a young man or boy).
example: Her youth and beauty attracted him to her.

definition: A locally circumscribed place characterized by some distinctive features.
etymology: From Latin zōna, from Ancient Greek ζώνη (zṓnē, “girdle, belt”). Doublet of zona.
